---
title: "Quiz: Hough transform for circles"
---

Short questions to test your understanding. Try each on paper first, then open the answer. A circle is $(x - a)^2 + (y - b)^2 = r^2$ in pixel coordinates; the accumulator holds votes per $(a, b, r)$, shown as the fraction of $2\pi r$.

---

**Q1.** With a known radius $r$, for which centres does a single edge point vote?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Where can the centre of a circle of radius $r$ through the point be?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
For every centre at distance $r$ from it: a ring of radius $r$ around the edge point. The rings of all points on a true circle of radius $r$ pass through its centre, which collects one vote per point.
:::

---

**Q2.** The radius is unknown, between 5 and 40 pixels. What does the accumulator look like, and what does one edge point vote for?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
One slice per radius.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
A 3D accumulator $(a, b, r)$: one $(a, b)$ slice per radius, 36 slices. An edge point votes for a ring of radius $r$ in slice $r$, for every $r$: a cone of votes. A circle is a 3D peak at its centre and radius.
:::

---

**Q3.** How does the gradient direction reduce the number of votes? What is "polarity" and why does it matter?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
In which direction is the centre seen from an edge point of a circle?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
On a circle the gradient is radial, so the centre lies on the line through the point along the gradient, at distance $r$: only two candidate centres per radius instead of a ring of about $2\pi r$. The polarity says whether the object is brighter than its surroundings (gradient points inward: centre at $\mathbf p + r\mathbf u$) or darker (outward: $\mathbf p - r\mathbf u$). If it is known, one vote per radius suffices; if it is wrong, every vote goes to the wrong side and nothing is found.
:::

---

**Q4.** You run the circle Hough transform with radius 15 on discs of radius 12. What do you see in the accumulator slice?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Where do rings of radius 15 around points of a circle of radius 12 overlap?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
No sharp peak. The rings of radius 15 around the points of a circle of radius 12 do not share a point; they overlap most along a ring of radius $15 - 12 = 3$ around the true centre (and more weakly on a ring of radius $15 + 12 = 27$). The slice shows bright small rings instead of peaks, and with a sensible threshold nothing is detected.
:::

---

**Q5.** Why does an ellipse give a weak, smeared peak, or two false circles, instead of one sharp peak?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Where are the centres of the circles that best fit the different parts of an ellipse?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Each part of the ellipse is best fitted by a circle of a different radius and centre (its centre of curvature): small circles near the pointed ends, a large circle along the flat sides. The votes spread over these centres and radii, so no bin collects the whole boundary. With a low threshold, the strongly curved ends can each produce a separate false circle.
:::

---

**Q6.** A plate has wells of one known radius. Why is that case much cheaper than detecting cells of unknown size?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
How many slices does the accumulator need?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
A known radius needs only one 2D slice instead of a stack of slices: the bins and the votes shrink by the number of radii. With gradient voting and known polarity each edge point casts exactly one vote.
:::

---

**Q7.** *(math)* Show that with a known radius the circle Hough accumulator is the correlation of the binary edge map with a ring-shaped kernel.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Write the vote count at a centre $\mathbf c$ as a sum over pixels.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
The centre $\mathbf c$ gets one vote from every edge pixel $\mathbf p$ with $\|\mathbf p - \mathbf c\| \approx r$: $H(\mathbf c) = \sum_{\mathbf p} E(\mathbf p)\,K(\mathbf p - \mathbf c)$ with $K(\mathbf d) = 1$ if $|\|\mathbf d\| - r| < \tfrac12$ and 0 otherwise. That is the correlation of $E$ with the ring $K$; since $K(\mathbf d) = K(-\mathbf d)$ it is also a convolution.
:::

---

**Q8.** *(math)* Why does a general ellipse have five parameters, and how large is a full ellipse accumulator with 50 steps per parameter?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
A conic $Ax^2 + Bxy + Cy^2 + Dx + Ey + F = 0$.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Six coefficients, defined only up to a common factor: 5 degrees of freedom (centre, two semi-axes, angle). A full accumulator has $50^5 = 312.5$ million bins, far too many; that is why ellipses are found centre-first or by hypothesise-and-verify.
:::
